title: Out-playing Herschel Thomas on 'Suitcase Blues' in Houston
summary: At an after-hours club Price plays Herschel Thomas's own solo and wins the room, then repeats it when Herschel follows him to Galveston.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: He was a blues player. Herschel and I were friends. And Herschel...women liked him, you know...so he always had two or three women following him around, so after the show one night we went to this after-hours club and when we got into this after-hours club, he tried to show me up by telling everybody how great a piano player he was, and that I couldn't play and this. But what I did, like Jesse Crump, Herschel Thomas, James P. Johnson, those famous solos, I had learned them. So I said, "Man, you don't want to mess with me," I said; "Herschel, you know I'm too, you know, I'm from 'the Big D' ." So finally he kept fooling around and fooling around, so I said, "Okay, I'll play." And when I sat down to play--he had made a famous solo on a Suitcase Blues." . I played that piano solo and all of the women just came to me, you

That was his...(Laughter). After I played his big number I went into my "Dallas Stomp"...you know what I mean...the blues, you know, this here, you know what I mean. I could really stomp because this girl had really...a week with her and I realized that that's what rhythm was, you know, that the rhythm was part of it...you didn't have girls, so it was the stomping... you know what I mean...it was the stomping in here and the combination of the piano and humming and all, then you were...then when I got through with that, that was the end of Mr. Herschel's time. He followed me from Houston to Galveston. And every time that he would do it...he didn't have sense enough to sit down and play the thing first. He's follow me to a town and when I'd sit right I'd say, "Herschel, I told you..." and I'd play the "Suitcase Blues." And they just couldn't believe it! And I think I broke his heart...you know what I mean...and then, by then, after the second week I was a veteran, you know. Then I could play the blues anyway, because I knew Jesse Crump's things, you know, and I could hear. See, I learned how to develop a system of chords...
